title: Why this firm, why this role
objectives: Answer "why trading" and "why us" with specific, true reasons.

screens.title: Three answers to "why us?"
screens.prose: Three candidates answer "Why us?" for the same trading firm. An interviewer hears dozens of these a week.

rows: Firm K is a world-leading firm with a great culture, and I want to work with the best.
Firm K is a leading global market maker that values innovation, teamwork and integrity.
At Firm K's campus talk, a trader showed how it quotes options all day. I built an options pricer in Python. I want to test that kind of pricing against live markets as a trader.

state.caption: Firm K is an invented market maker in Amsterdam that trades options. Answer B copies its careers page.

screens.question: Tap the strongest answer.

hints.text: Which answer could only be about this firm and this candidate?
Swap "Firm K" for another name: which answers still work?
A and B fit any firm. C names something the firm does and links it to the candidate's own work.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the answer that fits only this firm and this person.

byKey.r0: You picked the flattering answer. "World-leading" and "great culture" fit any firm.
byKey.r1: You picked the careers-page answer. The interviewer wrote that page and learns nothing new.

explain.text: Answers A and B would still work with any firm's name in them. Answer C names one thing Firm K does and links it to work the candidate did. It also says which role, and why.

screens.prose: Answer C has three parts: **a true, specific fact** about the firm and **a link to your own evidence**. The third is **why this role**, not another.

rows: Firm K quotes options all day (from its campus talk)
To test pricing against live markets, as a trader

screens.question: Which sentence of answer C fills the middle part?

options.text: "I built an options pricer in Python."
"A trader showed how it quotes options all day."
options.why: That is the fact about the firm, the first part.

options.text: "I want to test that kind of pricing as a trader."
options.why: That is why this role, the third part.

options.text: "Firm K is a world-leading firm."
options.why: That sentence is from answer A. It is flattery, not evidence.

hints.text: Which sentence is about the candidate, not the firm?
Evidence is something you did.
"I built an options pricer in Python" is the candidate's own work.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The middle part is about the candidate.

explain.text: The fact is about the firm, the evidence is about you, and the role links the two. Missing any one part makes the answer generic. The pricer is evidence because the interviewer can ask about it.

values.r1c1: Built an options pricer in Python

screens.prose: "Why trading?" and "why research?" need different reasons. Here are two true reasons from two candidates.

rows: I like quick decisions under uncertainty, with feedback the same day
I want to spend weeks answering one question with data

screens.question: Which fits a trader application?

options.text: Reason 1: quick decisions with feedback the same day
Reason 2: weeks on one question with data
options.why: You picked the researcher's reason. A trader's day is many small decisions, judged the same day.

options.text: Neither; say trading pays more
options.why: You chose pay. It tells the interviewer you would leave for a better offer.

options.text: Neither; say you follow the financial news
options.why: You chose the news. It shows an interest, not a reason, and several trading firms state no finance knowledge is needed.

hints.text: Which reason matches a trader's day in l1?
Traders decide many times a minute.
Reason 1 is the trader's; reason 2 is the researcher's.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the reason to the role's daily work.

explain.text: A trader makes many quick decisions and learns the same day whether they were good. A researcher spends weeks on one question. Give the reason that matches the role you are applying for.

screens.prose: The fact must be true, and you must be able to say where it came from. Here are six places candidates look.

rows: What the firm says it does
Someone you met at an event
A name, a date, one thing they said
A starting point, checked against the firm's page
The firm's place in a ranking

screens.question: Select all that apply: which give a fact you can use?

options.text: Careers and education pages
A talk or published material
Someone you met at an event
l4's dated table, checked against the firm's page
A forum rumour about bonuses
options.why: You used a rumour. You cannot say where it came from, and it is about pay.

options.text: The firm's place in a ranking
options.why: You used a ranking. It is prestige, and it says nothing about the work.

hints.text: Could you name the source if the interviewer asked?
Rumours and rankings fail that test.
The firm's pages, its talks, a person you met and l4's table, once checked. Not the rumour or the ranking.

feedback.correct: Four sources you could name aloud.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the sources you could name and defend.

explain.text: A usable fact has a source you can name: the firm's page, a talk, a person and a date. The table in l4 is dated October 2026, so check it on the firm's page first. Rumours and rankings are not facts about the work.

screens.prose: A "why us" answer should take about 45 seconds aloud. Speak at a calm 130 words a minute. Pace: when you practise, time it on a phone.
screens.question: About how many words is a 45-second answer?

hints.text: What fraction of a minute is 45 s?
Three quarters of a minute.
$130 \times 0.75 = 97.5$, about 100 words.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take three quarters of 130.

byKey.sec: You counted one word a second. Speech at 130 a minute is over two words a second.
byKey.full: That is a full minute. The answer is 45 seconds.

explain.text: Forty-five seconds is $0.75$ of a minute, and $130 \times 0.75 = 97.5$. As a check, 130 a minute is about 2.17 words a second, and $2.17 \times 45 \approx 97.5$. About 100 words: three or four sentences.

screens.prose: The same evidence can serve two firm types. Nadia's pricer fits a trading firm, as in answer C. Here she fits it to a bank's strats desk, whose interns build pricing tools.
screens.question: Put the paragraph's sentences in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: At the bank's insight evening, a strat showed the pricing tools its traders use with clients.
I built an options pricer in Python and checked it against 200 quoted prices.
Strats suits me because I want my code used by others every day.
I want to learn how a pricer is made safe enough for a trading desk.
I want to make fast trading decisions with my own risk limit.
lines.why: You kept a trader's reason. It argues for the other firm type.

hints.text: Fact, evidence, role, then what you want to learn.
One sentence is a reason to be a trader, not a strat.
Insight evening, pricer, why strats, what to learn. Drop the risk-limit sentence.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the three parts, then add what you want to learn.

byKey.d: You kept the trader's reason. On a strats paragraph it says you want a different job.
byKey.left-out: You left out a sentence that belongs. Only the risk-limit line goes.

explain.text: The evidence stayed the same; the fact and the role changed with the firm type. A strats desk wants code others rely on, so the role sentence says that. The trader's sentence would argue for a different job.

screens.prose: A candidate is asked "why us?" by a trading firm. The candidate has three reasons ready.

rows: The pay is the best in the industry
It is the most famous firm on my list
Its talk on options quoting matched the pricer I built

screens.question: Which reason should lead the answer?

options.text: Reason 3, the talk and the pricer
Reason 1, the pay
options.why: You led with pay.

options.text: Reason 2, the fame
options.why: You led with prestige.

options.text: All three, pay first
options.why: You opened with pay. The other two reasons never recover from it.

hints.text: How does an interviewer hear "the pay is the best"?
As "I would leave for more".
Lead with the specific reason; leave pay and fame out.

feedback.correct: The specific reason; pay and fame stay out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each reason tells the interviewer about you.

byKey.pay: You led with pay. Interviewers hear it as "would leave for more", and it says nothing about why this firm.
byKey.fame: You led with prestige. It says you chose the name, not the work.
byKey.all: You opened with pay. The interviewer stops listening for the good reason.

explain.text: Pay and prestige are true for many candidates, so they say nothing about you. Interviewers hear pay as "would leave for more". Lead with the specific fact and your evidence.

screens.prose: An edge case. A small firm on Nadia's list has a one-page website. She has found almost nothing about it.
screens.question: What should her "why us?" do?

options.text: Say what she checked and found, and what she wants to learn there; invent nothing
Make up a plausible fact about its strategy
options.why: You invented a fact. One follow-up question would expose it.

options.text: Say she knows nothing about the firm and stop
options.why: You gave up. Say what you checked and what you hope to learn.

options.text: Talk about the industry in general
options.why: You went generic. The answer would fit any firm.

hints.text: What does she actually know?
A small team trading futures.
Use that, say it came from the careers page, and say what she wants to learn.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use only what she checked.

explain.text: A small true fact beats an invented big one. "A small team trading futures" is enough, with what she hopes to learn there. Never invent a fact: interviewers know their own firm.

screens.prose: Every strong answer you picked had one shape: $$\text{why us} = \text{a true fact} + \text{your evidence} + \text{why this role}$$ It runs about 45 seconds: $130 \times \tfrac{45}{60} \approx 100$ words.

rows: Built an options pricer in Python
Test pricing against live markets as a trader

screens.question: Which answer has all three parts?

options.text: "Your talk showed a desk run on code. I wrote a dice-market simulator. I want a trading role where code and quick decisions meet."
"Your talk showed a desk run on code, and I want to trade there."
options.why: You picked an answer with no evidence. Nothing links the fact to the candidate.

options.text: "I wrote a dice-market simulator, so I want to trade."
options.why: You picked an answer with no fact about the firm. It fits any firm.

options.text: "Your talk showed a desk run on code, and I wrote a dice-market simulator."
options.why: You picked an answer with no role. Say why trading, not research.

hints.text: Check each answer for a fact, evidence and a role.
Three of them miss one part.
Only the first has the talk, the simulator and the role.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for all three parts.

explain.text: The first answer has the fact (the talk), the evidence (the simulator) and the role (trading). Each other answer drops one part. The missing part is what makes an answer generic.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** The trading firm's interviewer pushes: "Why us and not a hedge fund?" Pace: answer in about 20 seconds aloud.

rows: Quotes prices all day; feedback the same day
Tests ideas for weeks before they trade

screens.question: Which answer is strongest?

options.text: "I want to quote all day and know the same day if I was right. A research role spends weeks before an idea trades."
"I have applied to both."
options.why: Honest, but it does not answer the question. Say what draws you to this one.

options.text: "Hedge funds are worse places to work."
options.why: You ran down another firm type. Interviewers hear it as a judgement you cannot back up.

options.text: "I do not know much about hedge funds."
options.why: You admitted a gap without a reason for your choice.

hints.text: Compare the two days in the table.
Fast feedback is the trader's reason.
Name the difference that matters to you, without running anyone down.

feedback.correct: A real difference, said without running anyone down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the difference that draws you.

explain.text: The strongest answer names a real difference between the two jobs. It ties that difference to what the candidate wants, as in the trader's reason. It never criticises the other firm type.

screens.prose: Draft your own three reasons in your head first. Then mark this model paragraph by Nadia, an invented candidate, for Firm M, an invented London trading firm.

lines: At Firm M's insight evening in October, a trader showed how it quotes exchange-traded funds all day.
I run my university's poker society, and I log every hand's expected value in a spreadsheet.
That is why trading, not research: I like fast decisions with feedback the same day.
I want to learn how Firm M sizes its quotes when markets move quickly.

screens.question: Select all that apply: which rubric lines does the paragraph meet?

options.text: Names a true, specific fact with where it came from
Links it to her own evidence
Says why this role, not another
Says what she wants to learn there
Gives pay as a reason
options.why: You ticked pay. The paragraph never mentions it, which is right.

options.text: Praises the firm's culture
options.why: You ticked flattery. There is none, which is why it works.

hints.text: Read the paragraph line by line against the rubric.
Line 1 is the fact, line 2 the evidence.
Line 3 gives the role and line 4 what she wants to learn. No pay, no flattery.

feedback.correct: Four rubric lines met. You write three in homework 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each line to a rubric point.

explain.text: Line 1 gives the fact and its source; line 2 the evidence. Line 3 gives the role and line 4 what she wants to learn, in about 60 words. You write three of your own, for real firms, in homework 2.

ideas: A "why us" answer is a true, specific fact, a link to your own evidence, and why this role.
Facts come from sources you can name: the firm's pages, a talk, a person met at an event.
About 45 seconds aloud, about 100 words. Pay, prestige and flattery are never the reason.

quiz.question: Which fact can you use in a "why us" answer?

options.text: What a trader said at the firm's campus talk last week, with the date
A forum post about its bonuses
options.why: You used a rumour about pay.

options.text: Its place in a top-ten list

quiz.question: Your "why us" draft is 250 words. About how long is that aloud at 130 words a minute?

feedback.correct: About 115 seconds, more than twice the target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by 130, then turn minutes into seconds.

byKey.min: That is in minutes. The question asks for seconds.

explain.text: $250 / 130 \approx 1.92$ minutes, and $1.92 \times 60 \approx 115$ seconds. The target is 45 seconds, so cut it to about 100 words.

quiz.question: Why do interviewers mark down "the pay is the best"?

options.text: It suggests you would leave for a better offer
Because it is never true
options.why: It may be true. The problem is what it says about you.

options.text: Because talking about money is rude
options.why: It is not about manners. Pay tells them nothing about your fit for the work.

feedback.correct: It says you would leave for more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the reason predicts about you.

explain.text: A reason that is about pay predicts you will move when pay does. A reason about the work predicts you will stay and learn.
